To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the overexpression of cytoskeletal vinculin in cultured neonatal rat myocytes does not protect against ischemia-reperfussion injury.
overexpression of vinculine does not protect neonatal ventricular myocytes from ischemia-reperfusin injury.
increased expression of vinculn in the cytoskeleton does not protect neonatal rat cardiac myocytes from simulated ischemia-reperfuision injury.
In summary, our research is concerned with
ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury in cardiac tissue and the role of the cytoskeleton in this process.
the development of new strategies to reduce ischemia-reperfuson injury.
the role of cytoskeletal proteins, specifically vinculin, in the pathogenesis of I/R injury.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
increased expression of vinculine does not provide protection from ischemia reperfusion injury.
increased levels of vinculins do not protect ventricular myocytes from ischemia-reperfuson injury, and that the loss of vinculins does not appear to be the primary cause of I/R injury.
the increased expression of vincullin in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes does not provide protection from simulated I/R injury.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
vinculin is an important protein in the cell and that the loss of vinculiin may be an indicator of irreversible injury.
increased vinculin expression in the cytoskeleton does not protect myocytes from I/R injury and that hypothermic I/R is more protective than normothermic I/R.
vinculin does not protect the heart from I/R injury.

hypothermia is protective in neonatal rat myocytes.
